title: Right-Angled Trigonometry

findings.finding: Generalise the relationships between ratios for the two acute angles.
findings.breakdown: The existing question supplies all six ratios; explaining their relationships develops the angle-relative meaning of opposite and adjacent.
findings.checked: p6-guided-a and p6-guided-b already demonstrate exchanging the reference angle. For positive legs O and A, the complementary tangent ratios are O/A and A/O, whose product is 1.
findings.assumptions: Both reference angles are acute angles of a non-degenerate right triangle.

repair.proposal: After p7-q2, add an optional task: Compare sin θ with cos α, cos θ with sin α, and tan θ with tan α. Predict whether these relationships hold in every right-angled triangle, then explain using side lengths O, A and H relative to θ. Expected answer: the legs exchange opposite and adjacent roles, so sin θ = cos α = O/H and cos θ = sin α = A/H. The tangent ratios are O/A and A/O, so tan θ × tan α = 1.

findings.doneWhen: Students explain the relationships through side roles rather than numerical coincidence.

findings.finding: Question 11c requires relating two symbolic side lengths before any side can be calculated numerically, a setup not supplied by preceding instruction.
findings.breakdown: Unlike 11a and 11b, neither triangle has a known complete side. Students must express both top lengths in the shared unknown x and equate their difference to 10.
findings.checked: p26-teaching-method and p26-example-block model solving one triangle from a known side. p29-q8 and p30-q10 require multiple numerical calculations. p30-q11-a and p30-q11-b introduce shared triangles but retain a numerical starting route. No earlier teaching supplies the symbolic difference setup. The proposed equation gives x approximately 7.7, consistent with the diagram.
findings.assumptions: Students know ordinary linear equations and use a scientific calculator in degree mode. The final challenge position does not supply the missing equation setup.

repair.proposal: Add to 11c: “Express the whole top length and the shorter top length in terms of x using tangent. Their difference is 10; use this to form an equation for x.” The resulting equation is x/tan25° − x/tan50° = 10.

findings.doneWhen: The question supplies the route from the two triangles to one equation while students still select and rearrange the ratios.

findings.finding: The first isosceles task requires students to construct a right triangle without preceding instruction showing that construction.
findings.breakdown: In p34-q7-b, students must introduce an altitude and halve the base before using cosine. In p35-q12-h, they must recognise that the supplied altitude halves the apex angle. Applying a ratio to the whole triangle would use 6 instead of 3, or 70° instead of 35°.
findings.checked: Earlier teaching supplies side identification and trigonometric solving only in already identified right triangles. p34-q7-a adds an exterior-angle calculation but supplies no auxiliary construction. Ordinary isosceles properties taught elsewhere do not themselves model choosing this construction for trigonometry. The correct reductions give cos θ = 3/10 and x = 30cos35°.
findings.assumptions: Students know basic isosceles geometry, but the supplied booklet has not taught its application through an auxiliary right triangle.

repair.proposal: Add to p34-q7-b: “Draw a perpendicular from the apex to the base. In an isosceles triangle it bisects both the base and the apex angle. Label each half of the base 6÷2 = 3, then use one of the right triangles.”

findings.doneWhen: The first isosceles task explicitly establishes the construction and half-base, and prepares students to halve the apex angle in p35-q12-h.

findings.finding: Expose the seconds boundary and the carry into degrees through a controlled comparison.
findings.breakdown: The existing practice includes rounding up and down but does not compare values across the 30-second boundary when minutes are 59.
findings.checked: p38-rounding-block explicitly teaches both the 30-second threshold and carrying 60 minutes into degrees. All proposed answers follow that rule.
findings.assumptions: Use the booklet's convention that halfway values round up.

repair.proposal: After p39-q4, ask students to predict which answers will match, then round to the nearest minute: 42°59′10″, 42°59′29″, 42°59′30″, 42°59′50″. Expected answers: 42°59′, 42°59′, 43°0′, 43°0′. Ask what changes at 30 seconds and why the degree changes. Only seconds vary; degrees and minutes stay fixed. Follow with: Round 18°23′46″ to the nearest minute. Expected answer: 18°24′.

findings.doneWhen: Students explain both the rounding threshold and the carry into the next degree.

findings.finding: The topic lacks an opening rehearsal of side identification, sine and cosine selection, numerator and denominator rearrangement, and inverse-sine solving used directly in its examples.
findings.breakdown: Students must recover these substantial earlier methods while learning DMS calculator input and output. The immediately preceding topic rehearses conversion and rounding, not these trigonometric steps.
findings.checked: p21-teaching-block, p25-example-demonstration, p26-example-block and p31-example-block teach the methods earlier. p37–p39 rehearse DMS conversion and rounding. p40's examples directly use sine and cosine with unknowns in the numerator and denominator; p41's example directly uses inverse sine. Tangent and inverse cosine are removed from the claimed missing review because they are not steps in these worked examples.
findings.assumptions: Scientific calculator use is explicit. Calculator evaluation itself is not a missing review piece.

repair.proposal: Before p40-information-block, insert this short review: (1) Triangle ABC is right-angled at C, with reference angle A. Label AB, AC and BC as H, A or O. (2) Write the appropriate trigonometric equation: angle 35°, O=x, H=12; angle 40°, A=8, H=x. (3) Solve those two equations for x to 2 d.p. (4) Given O=6 and H=10, write the equation for θ and find θ to 2 d.p. Expected answers: H, A, O; sin35°=x/12 and cos40°=8/x; x≈6.88 and x≈10.44; sinθ=6/10 and θ≈36.87°. These four short items fit within one page.

findings.doneWhen: The opening review rehearses the prior trigonometric decisions and equation-solving methods used by the worked examples.

findings.finding: Contrast decimal-degree and degree-minute inputs with matching digit strings.
findings.breakdown: The comparison makes visible that minutes represent sixtieths rather than hundredths of a degree.
findings.checked: p37 teaches conversion and p40-information-block demonstrates equivalent decimal and DMS calculator inputs. The proposed decimal angles are 30°6′, 30°12′ and 30°18′, respectively; each is smaller than its paired DMS angle. All angles are acute, and each DMS cosine is smaller.
findings.assumptions: Students use degree mode and the taught DMS input method.

repair.proposal: Immediately after p40-information-block, ask students to predict which pairs have equal cosine values, then calculate to 4 d.p.: (1) cos30.10° and cos30°10′; (2) cos30.20° and cos30°20′; (3) cos30.30° and cos30°30′. Only the fractional digit string varies; the comparison of decimal notation with minute notation stays fixed. Expected answer: no pair is equal; each DMS angle is larger and its cosine smaller. The decimal angles convert to 30°6′, 30°12′ and 30°18′. Follow with: Write 42°24′ in decimal degrees, then evaluate its tangent using both forms. Expected answer: 42.4°, with equal tangent values.

findings.doneWhen: Students distinguish matching written digits from equivalent angle values.

findings.finding: Use the established altitude relationship to find the greatest height for a fixed hypotenuse.
findings.breakdown: The task extends the existing symbolic result h²=ab into a bound and an equality condition.
findings.checked: p53-q21 establishes h²=ab. With a,b>0 and a+b=L, (a−b)²≥0 gives L²≥4h², hence h≤L/2. Equality requires a=b; the two smaller right triangles then have equal legs, giving 45° acute angles in QPS.
findings.assumptions: Ordinary expansion and rearrangement of algebraic expressions are prior knowledge, consistent with the course's separate algebra booklets. All lengths are positive.

repair.proposal: After p53-q21-root, add an optional task: “Suppose QS=L is fixed. Using a+b=L and h²=ab, show that h cannot exceed L/2. Hint: start with (a−b)²≥0. When does equality occur, and what are the acute angles of triangle QPS?” Expected answer: (a+b)²≥4ab implies L²≥4h² and h≤L/2. Equality occurs when a=b=L/2; QPS is isosceles right-angled, with both acute angles 45°.

findings.doneWhen: Students derive the height bound and explain its equality case.
